I have somewhat different view than most having cut my options teeth on a dispersion book during the tech bubble.  

The index vol short half of the short correlation trade was always a choice in terms of its sizing.  Back then IV/RV premium was pretty narrow unlike today so every unit of Vega sold in index was managed carefully.  Being short index vol was a coin flip sort of trade.   The sizing ranged from Vega neutral to single stock book (which collected theta) to theta neutral which was Vega long. 

The drop in implied correlation makes the trade less attractive.  But given the level of implied on index the notable risk isn't selling index vol to low its buying single name vol way way too high.  The root causes of that single name vol levels are numerous including speculative demand and the dispersion trader competing to buy elevated single name vol.  the seller is absent and gets a sweet risk premium when providing any liquidity. The risk the dispersionis at most risk to is a single name vol  collapse.  Perhaps a large equity drawdown would also be a negative single name vol event but that seems pretty unlikely.  So then it comes down to hedging index level and sizing.  

Is the CIO buying index puts to hedge the dispersion traders?  Jeez maybe but then the LP's are just long single name vol at extremely elevated levels.  

My picture is of course if macro drives index levels down index implied will get bid up but on the day so will single name vol.  

Frankly the responsible CIO would be finding ways to get short single name vol if they are really worried NOT buying index puts at 20+ vol

But mostly I don't see them hedging much at all

The easiest way to understand what's happening in the markets is to think about 2008 and the collapse of Lehman Brothers.

That was the time Wall Street packaged and sold ridiculously risky products tied to housing bubble speculation.

They called these MBS and CDOs. And hen those unraveled everything crashed.

In 2026 the AI bubble has its equivalent for data center funding. But it's not the same scale yet. Although fears are surfacing.

This time they call it GPU-backed loans. And they go so far as to set up separate bankruptcy remote companies to own the GPUs.

Despite its junk rating CoreWeave for instance got an investment grade GPU loan at 6% because lenders priced in Meta's credit.

This borrowed credit opens the door to pension funds and insurers. Now GPU loans are being bundled into asset-backed bonds with AAA-rated tranches.

This time isn't different. Risks that start out isolated in one corner of the market can quickly become systemic. That's exactly how 2008 started.

This isn’t a coincidence. Europe is beginning to coalesce around a scheme to tax foreign AI firms in an effort to recoup a fiscal shortfall brought on by AI. It probably won’t work, but it makes sense: 

- AI tilts the factor share of income away from labor towards capital. Not the whole way, it’s just not 70/30 any more (70 being labor). Maybe it’s 60/40. This should be obvious. This doesn’t mean output falls. Probably output and productivity rise, it’s just that capital captures a larger share. 

- this fundamentally challenges the way developed states collect tax which is mainly on labor and wages. European nations in particular rely on personal income, payroll taxes and social contributions to fund grossly engorged welfare states. States must make up the lost payroll taxes by capturing the gains accruing to capital. But wait! Capital is a foreign AI firm. The AI firm disrupting domestic labor is probably not domestic in origin (for Europe). So there’s nothing left to tax. 

- European nations are mainly consumers rather than producers of AI. A producer nation has a similar problem - it must tax capital more aggressively to make up for lost labor income, but this is tractable - but a consumer nation has a much worse problem. Europe will face the substitution of domestic labor for foreign inference which benefits the owners of a largely foreign AI supply chain. When a French professional services firm gets disrupted and loses 70% of its staff due to AI productivity gain, the French government can’t tax Anthropic over in California to make up for the lost payroll and personal income taxes. The laid off French workers will also spend less reducing consumption tax receipts domestically. 

Some savings will remain in France as consumer surplus via lower prices but that’s not easily taxable. The French firm itself might be more profitable after it replaces staff with AI, and that is captured but that doesn’t make up the shortfall. 

- Europe has a few options. They will attempt all of them. They can a) regulate away AI disruption by banning AI use in professional fields. They can b) try and capture the tilt towards capital by fostering their own domestic industry of AI firms. They can c) try and extract rents from the foreign AI firms that are disrupting them. 

A) is the obvious move, make it illegal for an AI model to provide medical, legal, or accounting advice (etc). This will be very unpopular in the end but it will definitely be attempted. This is already underway. It will make these countries less productive and less competitive in the global market. And it wont work. People will find ways to use frontier AI. Diffusion will be slower but not inhibited. This will worsen Europe's fiscal situation overall by making it a worse place to do business and putting a drag on growth.

B) is another obvious move – if Anthropic is disrupting French white collar labor, ban Anthropic and support a domestic competitor - the Le Gros Chaton model or whatever. The only problem is that Europe appears incapable of creating a frontier model. They have the talent but not the right regulatory model or incentive to form capital locally. AI could have been invented in Europe, and many of its component parts and researchers are European, but the winning AI firms were largely not capitalized there, because of the exact thing we're talking about - an engorged welfare state and a high tax burden required to support it. Also, Europe has engaged in suicidal deindustrialization so it isn't competitive when it comes to the more fundamental inputs to AI like power and data centers. Thus, Europe will mainly be an importer and consumer of inference rather than a seller. Structurally, Europe will not be able to marshal capital locally which it could then shift the fiscal burden onto. European firms will continue to consume foreign inference. 

C) is where we land, and this explains Europe's behavior with these new exotic taxes on internet use and AI. Europe will have to contrive a way to try and recoup lost labor taxes by taxing foreign capital. American tech companies tolerate this for now as a nuisance cost of doing business in Europe, but this will eventually reach a fever pitch as Europe continues to raise the stakes. Want access to the European market? Pay us $10b/year in "fines" (taxes). Now pay us $100b a year. At some point, Europe will exhaust American tech companies' ability to pay and they will exit the market. Moreover, this is only a partial measure and depends on a benevolent America tolerating ankle-biting without taking punitive measures. The US has already begun applying pressure to Europe to stop coattail-riding via NATO and this will only accelerate, so Europe will have a very limited ability to extract fines. This won't work in the end, but expect to hear a lot about it in the coming years. 

In the end, Europe will benefit from AI as productivity gains diffuse throughout society, but AI will further deteriorate its already tenuous fiscal situation. Europe cannot cope with a situation in which domestic labor is outsourced to foreign inference, and it has an extremely limited ability to deal with this. I don't expect total collapse, but a continued erosion in standards of living and relevance, especially if they don't make the hard choices of slashing immigration, massive welfare states, and spending on the elderly.

This isn’t a coincidence. Europe is beginning to coalesce around a scheme to tax foreign AI firms in an effort to recoup a fiscal shortfall brought on by AI. It probably won’t work, but it makes sense: 

- AI tilts the factor share of income away from labor towards capital. Not the whole way, it’s just not 70/30 any more (70 being labor). Maybe it’s 60/40. This should be obvious. This doesn’t mean output falls. Probably output and productivity rise, it’s just that capital captures a larger share. 

- this fundamentally challenges the way developed states collect tax which is mainly on labor and wages. European nations in particular rely on personal income, payroll taxes and social contributions to fund grossly engorged welfare states. States must make up the lost payroll taxes by capturing the gains accruing to capital. But wait! Capital is a foreign AI firm. The AI firm disrupting domestic labor is probably not domestic in origin (for Europe). So there’s nothing left to tax. 

- European nations are mainly consumers rather than producers of AI. A producer nation has a similar problem - it must tax capital more aggressively to make up for lost labor income, but this is tractable - but a consumer nation has a much worse problem. Europe will face the substitution of domestic labor for foreign inference which benefits the owners of a largely foreign AI supply chain. When a French professional services firm gets disrupted and loses 70% of its staff due to AI productivity gain, the French government can’t tax Anthropic over in California to make up for the lost payroll and personal income taxes. The laid off French workers will also spend less reducing consumption tax receipts domestically. 

Some savings will remain in France as consumer surplus via lower prices but that’s not easily taxable. The French firm itself might be more profitable after it replaces staff with AI, and that is captured but that doesn’t make up the shortfall. 

- Europe has a few options. They will attempt all of them. They can a) regulate away AI disruption by banning AI use in professional fields. They can b) try and capture the tilt towards capital by fostering their own domestic industry of AI firms. They can c) try and extract rents from the foreign AI firms that are disrupting them. 

A) is the obvious move, make it illegal for an AI model to provide medical, legal, or accounting advice (etc). This will be very unpopular in the end but it will definitely be attempted. This is already underway. It will make these countries less productive and less competitive in the global market. And it wont work. People will find ways to use frontier AI. Diffusion will be slower but not inhibited. This will worsen Europe's fiscal situation overall by making it a worse place to do business and putting a drag on growth.

B) is another obvious move – if Anthropic is disrupting French white collar labor, ban Anthropic and support a domestic competitor - the Le Gros Chaton model or whatever. The only problem is that Europe appears incapable of creating a frontier model. They have the talent but not the right regulatory model or incentive to form capital locally. AI could have been invented in Europe, and many of its component parts and researchers are European, but the winning AI firms were largely not capitalized there, because of the exact thing we're talking about - an engorged welfare state and a high tax burden required to support it. Also, Europe has engaged in suicidal deindustrialization so it isn't competitive when it comes to the more fundamental inputs to AI like power and data centers. Thus, Europe will mainly be an importer and consumer of inference rather than a seller. Structurally, Europe will not be able to marshal capital locally which it could then shift the fiscal burden onto. European firms will continue to consume foreign inference. 

C) is where we land, and this explains Europe's behavior with these new exotic taxes on internet use and AI. Europe will have to contrive a way to try and recoup lost labor taxes by taxing foreign capital. American tech companies tolerate this for now as a nuisance cost of doing business in Europe, but this will eventually reach a fever pitch as Europe continues to raise the stakes. Want access to the European market? Pay us $10b/year in "fines" (taxes). Now pay us $100b a year. At some point, Europe will exhaust American tech companies' ability to pay and they will exit the market. Moreover, this is only a partial measure and depends on a benevolent America tolerating ankle-biting without taking punitive measures. The US has already begun applying pressure to Europe to stop coattail-riding via NATO and this will only accelerate, so Europe will have a very limited ability to extract fines. This won't work in the end, but expect to hear a lot about it in the coming years. 

In the end, Europe will benefit from AI as productivity gains diffuse throughout society, but AI will further deteriorate its already tenuous fiscal situation. Europe cannot cope with a situation in which domestic labor is outsourced to foreign inference, and it has an extremely limited ability to deal with this. I don't expect total collapse, but a continued erosion in standards of living and relevance, especially if they don't make the hard choices of slashing immigration, massive welfare states, and spending on the elderly.

Binance hack:

Largest ever crypto hack - from total 6bn, 3bn was frozen (good ratio imo). Binance is plugging the 3bn hole from their own balance sheet and SAFU fund (which is now fully depleted after this)

Its hard to see this event as positive for crypto, the cybersecurity FUD headlines just keep coming. Many people and institutions will now think even harder before entering the space. That being said its remarkable how small the dump was post-hack.

In parallel tech/ AI stocks are dumping as well and BTC is now less volatile than stocks, despite the news. 

I don’t want to sound premature but steady price action in face of big bad news suggests we are bottoming.

The industry wide reaction was quite professional this time, fast communication, USDT and USDC promptly frozen, Aave disabled all the pools to prevent hacker from using them. 

Cautiously optimistic the crypto industry will be hardened through all of these trials by fire and become much more resilient over time.

Otoh its very hard for me to make a case for buying a lot of crypto here, as cybersec is continuing to be an issue across board from exchanges, HW wallets, internet infra etc. 

Gun to head Id actually say its slightly bullish BTC here, just because it does seem its bottomed out, priced in all the FUD remarkably well and it’s the simplest exposure to crypto with smallest attack surface / complexity (sans some quantum/AI breaking cryptography tail event). 

So if any macro situation starts favoring crypto, it should favor BTC first, but it probably pays to wait for midterms to rip the "dems are coming for our coins" bandaid off.

NYSE/ICE + Druck + TradeXYZ/Hyperliquid

ICE and Druckenmiller are working with TradeXYZ to bring Hyperliquid perps to US. The announcement pumped HYPE by 15% (victory lap)

My initial gut reaction is that its bearish other competitors in this arena - e.g. LIT and ZRO - but I slept on it and start to lean bullish for everyone. ICE just fired the first shot but they are not exclusively working with TradeXYZ, they are massive investor in Polymarket, already work with LayerZero's ATLAS etc. etc.

ICE competitors and other institutions heard the shot and will now enter the arms race even faster (feeling FOMO / fear of being disrupted) and will try to bring their own guns to the fight. 

Some of them will perhaps also tap Hyperliquid, but its reasonable to assume some will want to differentiate and compete with different partners.

So in general bullish HYPE (and better yet PURR going above 1 mNAV same to CYPH on ZEC run), and bullish the whole "perps + tokenisation with US institutions" basket - LIT, ZRO, BP etc

However we should recalibrate this view after the midterms dust settles. Depending on how exactly they end and what the political rhetorics will be after.

We could see anything from mild impact (dems will ignore crypto to focus on AI, or they will silently support it seeing the adoption as inevitable) 

to severe (crypto will be a poster child of Trump&Co shenannigans that mustn't go unpunished)

Its fair to think many institutions are waiting for this signal

If you want to see what the future of housing looks like just look at economies that are already there

Tokyo, Seoul, Shanghai etc

What you see is apartments in the centre that are modern hotel style (not the old brick ones) with convenience and amenities are more expensive than houses an outside of a few special neighbourhoods most people prefer to live in convenient high amenity towers and ACTIVELY prefer it to owning a middle level house thats inconvenient in location - in many of these places even socially the automatic assumption (although not always) is that when someone says they live in a house is that they are poorer than someone who lives in high end apartment neighbourhoods

Once you travel out a while the homes are very cheap - in the west you havent seen that as much as demographics hold up via immigration etc but inevitably when demographics also decline people shift inward to centres leaving outer areas unfavourable

If you watch youtube or have experienced people you know many deca, centi millionaires who have lived in huge homes sell after a few years realising the upkeep in personnel, maintenance etc is just a mental headache separate to financial reasons

Thats how people increasingly feel these days with even modest old homes today - not well located so have to own a car, longer commute, cant walk to local shops and on top of that the house needs lot of money to fix and to top it all off they cant afford it either and these dynamics all shift the culture

The thing people say here is that its cope because young people cant afford and I can assure you its not true this is based on the old inconvenient apartments of the boomer years- young global people increasingly want lockup and leave with great amenities low maintenance. The young people that still want that are generally told that by their parents - sayings like "who wants to live an a shoe box"etc

In the west you can already see this in many city centres but it takes time to fully shift

If you are going to buy a place to live then dont worry about any of this just buy what you like - as you would a car it doesnt matter if it goes down in value its just for personal use
